Degenerate
dē-jĕn´ẽr-āt
v. and adj. (to fall away from the qualities of one's kind; grown worse than the stock one came from)
Latin degenerare, from de-, down from, and genus, race or kind — to fall away from one's kind. Jeremiah's vine is the governing figure.

Biblical Definition

To degenerate is to fall away from what one's kind should be. Jeremiah's figure is exact: “Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed: how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?” (Jer 2:21). Isaiah puts it in metal: “Thy silver is become dross, thy wine mixed with water” (Isa 1:22). The Lord charges a working, patient, orthodox church with it: “Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love” (Rev 2:4). Paul asks the Galatians the direct question: “Having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?” (Gal 3:3). And Hosea names the worst feature: “gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not” (Hos 7:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines degenerate as to fall from a perfect or good state into a less excellent or worse state; to become of a lower type than the parent stock.

expand to see more

DEGENERATE, v.i. To become of a lower type; to fall from a perfect or good state into a less excellent or worse state; to be or grow worse.

DEGENERATE, a. Having fallen from a perfect or good state into a less excellent or worse state; having lost something of the good qualities possessed; having declined in natural or moral worth.

Key Scripture

Jer 2:21 — "Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed: how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?"

Isa 1:22 — "Thy silver is become dross, thy wine mixed with water:"

Rev 2:4 — "Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love."

Gal 3:3 — "Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?"

Hos 7:9 — "Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knoweth it not: yea, gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not."

Modern Corruption

Decline is expected to announce itself, and the Bible's picture is of a man who does not know it has happened.

expand to see more

Hosea 7:9 is the most unnerving verse on the subject and it takes two clauses. Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knoweth it not; gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not. The repetition is the message. Degeneration is not experienced from the inside as a fall; it is experienced as normal, because the standard degrades along with the thing being measured. A church does not usually feel itself growing cold. It feels itself being reasonable, and only an outside measure — Scripture, or an older saint, or a comparison with what it once was — can register the change.

Revelation 2 is the case study, and its details should end any complacency built on activity. The Ephesian church had works, labour, patience, could not bear evil men, had tried false apostles and found them liars, had borne and not fainted. By every visible metric it was the soundest church on the list — and the Lord says I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love, and threatens to remove its candlestick. Doctrinal vigilance and hard work had continued after the love that produced them had gone, which is exactly how degeneration hides.

The remedy given in Revelation 2:5 is worth noting for its shape: remember, repent, and do the first works. It begins with memory, because a man who does not know he has declined cannot repent of it, and it ends with action rather than feeling — do the first works. Jeremiah 2:21 says the same thing about origin: God planted a noble vine, wholly a right seed, and the strange vine is a departure from what was given rather than a failure to achieve something new. Recovery in Scripture is nearly always a return.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sur (H5494), degenerate, turned aside; sig (H5509), dross; Greek enarchomai / epiteleo (G1728, G2005), to begin / to complete; aphiemi (G863), to leave, let go.

expand to see more

Hebrew surey haggephen (H5494) — the degenerate shoots of the vine; Jeremiah 2:21 only.

Hebrew sig (H5509) — dross; Isaiah 1:22, 1:25, Psalm 119:119, Proverbs 25:4.

Greek aphekas (G863) — thou hast left; Revelation 2:4 — left, not lost.

Usage

"“Gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not” — twice, he knoweth not."

"“Thou hast left thy first love” — said to the busiest church on the list."

"“Remember… repent, and do the first works” — memory first, then action."
